title: Timeline Basics
conceptGoal: Understand how clips, tracks and the playhead work together so a timeline edit is predictable instead of accidental.

questions.prompt: What does a ripple delete do that a plain delete does not?
options: It removes the clip and closes the gap by shifting later clips left
It removes the clip and leaves a gap of the same length
It removes only the audio of the clip
It removes the clip from the media pool as well
questions.explanation: A ripple delete edits the timeline as a chain: removing the clip pulls everything after it earlier, so total duration shrinks and no blank gap is left behind.

questions.prompt: You set an in point and an out point on a source clip. What have you defined?
options: The part of the source that will be inserted into the timeline
The export range of the final render
The clip's playback speed
The clip's position on the track
questions.explanation: In and out points mark a sub-range of the source media, and only that range is taken when you insert or overwrite into the timeline.

questions.prompt: Why are higher video tracks drawn on top in a standard NLE?
options: Because layers composite top-down, so the highest opaque track wins
Because higher tracks always render at higher resolution
Because lower tracks are muted automatically
Because only track 1 accepts effects
questions.explanation: Video tracks are a compositing stack. The topmost opaque pixel is what you see, which is why titles and overlays live above the base footage.

questions.prompt: A three-point edit needs how many of the four in/out points set by hand?
options: Three
Four
Two
One
questions.explanation: You set three points (typically source in and out plus a timeline in) and the NLE derives the fourth from the clip duration, so the edit lands deterministically.

title: Cuts and Transitions
conceptGoal: Understand when a hard cut is the right choice and what a dissolve actually communicates to the viewer.

questions.prompt: What does a cross dissolve most commonly signal to an audience?
options: A passage of time or a change of place
That the next shot is more important
That the footage was shot on a different camera
That the film is about to end
questions.explanation: A dissolve overlaps two shots in time, and audiences have been trained by convention to read that overlap as elapsed time or a scene change.

questions.prompt: What is a J-cut?
options: The audio of the next shot starts before its picture
The picture of the next shot starts before its audio
A cut made exactly on a beat of music
A cut that reverses screen direction
questions.explanation: In a J-cut the incoming audio leads the incoming picture, which pulls the viewer into the next scene before they see it and smooths the transition.

questions.prompt: Why does cutting on action tend to feel invisible?
options: The motion carries the eye across the cut so the splice is not noticed
Because the two shots have identical color
Because the cut is always shorter than four frames
Because the audio is muted at the cut point
questions.explanation: The viewer is tracking a continuing movement, so their attention is on the action rather than on the frame where the shot changed.

title: Blender Navigation
conceptGoal: Understand Blender's viewport, the split between object and edit mode, and how transforms are applied.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between Object Mode and Edit Mode?
options: Object Mode transforms whole objects; Edit Mode changes the mesh's vertices, edges and faces
Object Mode is for rendering; Edit Mode is for exporting
Object Mode disables the viewport; Edit Mode enables it
They are the same thing with different shortcuts
questions.explanation: Object Mode operates on the object as a single unit through its transform, while Edit Mode operates on the geometry inside it, so the same move key produces very different results.

questions.prompt: Why does applying scale matter before adding a modifier like Bevel?
options: Unapplied scale makes the modifier's distances behave non-uniformly
Modifiers cannot be added to scaled objects at all
Applying scale doubles the render speed
It converts the mesh to a curve
questions.explanation: Modifiers work in the object's local space, so a non-uniform object scale stretches their distances; applying scale resets the scale to 1 and makes widths behave as typed.

questions.prompt: What does the origin point of an object control?
options: The pivot for rotation and scaling, and the object's reported location
The colour of the object in the viewport
Which collection the object belongs to
The render resolution of the object
questions.explanation: Transforms are computed relative to the origin, so an origin far from the geometry makes rotation swing the object around instead of spinning it in place.

title: Shot Sizes and Framing
conceptGoal: Understand how shot size changes the emotional distance between the audience and the subject.

questions.prompt: A wide shot placed at the start of a scene mainly does what?
options: Establishes geography so later close-ups make spatial sense
Hides continuity errors in the close-ups
Shortens the scene's runtime
Forces the viewer to read the subject's emotion
questions.explanation: The establishing wide gives the audience a mental map of the space; without it, tight shots feel disorienting because there is no context to place them in.

questions.prompt: Why does a longer focal length appear to compress depth?
options: It narrows the field of view, so foreground and background scale differences shrink
It physically moves the background closer
It increases the sensor size
It raises the frame rate
questions.explanation: A narrow field of view crops to a small angular slice, so objects at different distances differ less in apparent size and the image reads as flattened.

questions.prompt: What is headroom?
options: The space between the top of the subject's head and the top of the frame
The dynamic range left before audio clips
The unused space on the timeline
The distance from the camera to the subject
questions.explanation: Headroom is a framing term: too much makes the subject sink in frame, too little feels cramped, so it is a deliberate compositional choice rather than an accident.

title: Audio Levels and Loudness
conceptGoal: Understand the difference between peak level and perceived loudness, and why mixes are delivered to a loudness target.

questions.prompt: Two clips both peak at -3 dBFS but one sounds much louder. Why?
options: Perceived loudness depends on average energy over time, not on the single loudest peak
One clip has a higher sample rate
One clip is mono and mono is always louder
Peak meters are inaccurate above -6 dBFS
questions.explanation: Peak measures the highest instantaneous sample, while loudness in LUFS integrates energy over time, so a dense, compressed clip sits far louder at the same peak.

questions.prompt: What does 0 dBFS mean in a digital mix?
options: The maximum value the format can represent; going past it clips
A comfortable target level for dialogue
Digital silence
The noise floor of the recording
questions.explanation: dBFS is referenced to full scale, so 0 is the ceiling of the number format and samples that would exceed it are flattened, which is audible distortion.

questions.prompt: Why leave headroom when recording dialogue?
options: Unexpected loud moments can be recovered later, but clipped audio cannot
It makes the file smaller
It raises the sample rate automatically
It removes room tone
questions.explanation: Gain can be added in post without loss, but clipping destroys the waveform at capture time, so recording a little low is the recoverable mistake.

questions.prompt: What is room tone used for?
options: Filling gaps so silence between lines matches the scene's ambience
Boosting the dialogue level
Removing reverb from a recording
Synchronising picture and sound
questions.explanation: Digital silence next to a noisy recording is jarring, so room tone keeps the noise floor continuous and makes edits in the dialogue inaudible.

title: Sound Design Layers
conceptGoal: Understand how dialogue, effects, ambience and music occupy different roles so a mix stays readable.

questions.prompt: Dialogue is getting buried by music. What is the cleanest first fix?
options: Duck the music under the dialogue rather than pushing the dialogue louder
Raise the dialogue until it clips
Remove the music entirely
Convert everything to mono
questions.explanation: Intelligibility is about the relationship between elements, so lowering the competing element preserves the dialogue's natural level and the overall loudness target.

questions.prompt: What does ambience contribute to a scene?
options: A continuous sense of place that glues separate shots into one space
The rhythm the edit is cut to
The loudest element of the mix
Synchronised hard effects like footsteps
questions.explanation: Ambience is continuous rather than event-based, so it persists across cuts and makes a collection of shots feel like a single location.

questions.prompt: Why do sound effects often get exaggerated compared to reality?
options: Recorded reality under-delivers emotionally, so effects are designed for impact
Microphones cannot record real sounds
It reduces file size
It is required by broadcast standards
questions.explanation: The audience reads sound emotionally, so a designed, larger-than-life effect matches the felt weight of the action even though it is not literally accurate.

title: Color Correction Fundamentals
conceptGoal: Understand the difference between correction and grading, and how to read a waveform and a vectorscope.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between correction and grading?
options: Correction normalises the image; grading applies a deliberate look
Correction happens after grading
Correction only affects audio
Grading is automatic and correction is manual
questions.explanation: Correction gets shots to a neutral, matched baseline and grading is the creative pass on top, and doing them in that order keeps the look consistent across shots.

questions.prompt: A waveform monitor primarily shows you what?
options: The luminance distribution of the image against horizontal position in the frame
The hue of each pixel on a colour wheel
The audio level over time
The frame rate stability
questions.explanation: The waveform plots brightness per column, which is why it is the tool of choice for setting black point, white point and matching exposure between shots.

questions.prompt: On a vectorscope, what does the skin tone line indicate?
options: The hue axis natural skin tones should sit near regardless of ethnicity
The maximum legal saturation
The white balance of the lens
The gamma curve in use
questions.explanation: Skin tones cluster along one hue axis because they differ mainly in luminance and saturation, so that line is a reliable white balance and grading reference.

questions.prompt: Why grade in a log or wide-gamut working space when the footage allows it?
options: More tonal information survives heavy adjustments before banding appears
It makes exports faster
It removes the need for a vectorscope
It automatically matches shots
questions.explanation: Log encodings spread the captured dynamic range across code values more evenly, so pushing contrast later stretches data that is actually there instead of inventing it.

title: Pacing and Rhythm
conceptGoal: Understand how shot duration and cut density control tension, and why pacing is a story tool rather than a style.

questions.prompt: Why does shortening shots progressively raise tension?
options: The viewer gets less time to process each image, which feels like accelerating pressure
Shorter shots are always brighter
It reduces the total runtime
It forces the audio to duck
questions.explanation: Cut rate sets the viewer's cognitive workload, so as shots fall below comfortable reading time the sense of urgency rises even when the content is calm.

questions.prompt: A shot is held long after the action ends. What is the usual intent?
options: To give the audience space to feel the consequence
To pad the runtime for delivery
To hide a continuity error
To avoid using a transition
questions.explanation: Holding past the beat removes new information, so the audience's attention turns inward to the emotional aftermath rather than to what happens next.

questions.prompt: What usually determines where a cut lands in a dialogue scene?
options: Where the audience's attention naturally shifts, often to a reaction
The exact midpoint of the line
The first frame of every new shot in the bin
A fixed number of frames after the line ends
questions.explanation: The edit follows attention, so cutting when the viewer wants to look at the listener feels motivated while cutting on a metronome feels mechanical.

title: Keyframes and Easing
conceptGoal: Understand how interpolation between keyframes produces the timing and weight an animation is judged on.

questions.prompt: Linear interpolation between two keyframes looks robotic mainly because
options: Real motion accelerates and decelerates, and linear curves have constant velocity
Linear interpolation drops frames
It renders at a lower resolution
It always overshoots the target
questions.explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, which never happens to objects with mass, so the eye reads the motion as mechanical.

questions.prompt: What does the slope of an F-curve in the graph editor represent?
options: The rate of change of the animated value, that is its velocity
The render time of that frame
The opacity of the object
The number of keyframes remaining
questions.explanation: The curve plots value against time, so its slope is the derivative, which is why flat sections read as holds and steep sections as fast motion.

questions.prompt: Why add a small overshoot before settling on a pose?
options: It suggests momentum, so the motion reads as having mass
It shortens the animation
It prevents keyframe drift
It is required for looping
questions.explanation: Objects with inertia cannot stop instantly, so a slight overshoot and settle mimics that physical behaviour and makes the motion believable.

questions.prompt: What is anticipation in animation?
options: A small opposite movement before the main action
Rendering the next shot in advance
Holding the last frame longer
Animating on twos instead of ones
questions.explanation: A wind-up in the opposite direction prepares the viewer's eye and stores visible energy, which makes the main action land with more force.

title: Camera Movement with Intent
conceptGoal: Understand what each camera move communicates so movement is motivated rather than decorative.

questions.prompt: What is the visual difference between a dolly in and a zoom in?
options: A dolly changes perspective relationships; a zoom only magnifies the same perspective
A dolly is faster than a zoom
A zoom changes depth of field and a dolly never does
There is no difference on a virtual camera
questions.explanation: Moving the camera changes the distances between it and the objects, which alters parallax, while changing focal length only crops into the same viewpoint.

questions.prompt: Why should a camera move usually start and end on a composed frame?
options: Both ends are held on screen, so a weak frame at either end reads as a mistake
Because moves cannot be trimmed later
Because motion blur only works that way
Because the renderer requires static keyframes
questions.explanation: The static heads and tails are where the viewer actually reads composition, since the travel between them passes too quickly to redeem a bad start or stop.

questions.prompt: What does the 180-degree rule protect?
options: Consistent screen direction between characters across cuts
The exposure between shots
The audio phase between microphones
The frame rate of the sequence
questions.explanation: Keeping the camera on one side of the action line means characters stay on the same side of frame shot to shot, so the spatial relationship stays legible.

title: Shading and Materials
conceptGoal: Understand how a PBR shader's roughness, metallic and normal inputs describe a surface to the renderer.

questions.prompt: What does raising roughness do to a surface's specular response?
options: It scatters reflections into a wider, dimmer highlight
It makes reflections sharper and brighter
It removes reflections entirely
It changes only the base colour
questions.explanation: Roughness models microscopic surface irregularity, which spreads reflected rays over a wider cone, so the same energy is smeared into a soft highlight.

questions.prompt: Why should the metallic input usually be 0 or 1 rather than something in between?
options: Real materials are either conductors or dielectrics, so mid values are a blending hack
Values between 0 and 1 crash the renderer
Mid values double the render time
The shader ignores any value below 1
questions.explanation: Metalness is a physical classification rather than a dial, so intermediate values only make sense for texture masks blending two distinct materials across a surface.

questions.prompt: A normal map differs from a displacement map because
options: It fakes surface detail by perturbing shading normals without moving geometry
It only works on curves
It stores colour rather than direction
It is applied after rendering
questions.explanation: Normal maps change how light is calculated but leave the silhouette flat, which is why grazing angles and edges reveal the trick where real displacement would not.

questions.prompt: Why does UV unwrapping matter for texturing?
options: It defines how a 2D texture maps onto the 3D surface, controlling stretching and seams
It determines the polygon count
It sets the render sample count
It bakes lighting into the mesh
questions.explanation: Textures are 2D images, so the UV layout is the correspondence between image space and surface, and a bad unwrap stretches or repeats detail no matter how good the texture is.

title: Lighting a Subject
conceptGoal: Understand how key, fill and rim lights shape a subject and how light size controls shadow softness.

questions.prompt: What makes a shadow edge soft rather than hard?
options: The light source being large relative to the subject
The light being dimmer
The light being further away at the same physical size
A higher render sample count
questions.explanation: A large source illuminates the shadow boundary from many angles and creates a wide penumbra, while a point-like source leaves a sharp transition.

questions.prompt: What is the fill light's job?
options: To control how deep the shadows cast by the key light read
To separate the subject from the background
To provide the dominant direction of light
To light the background only
questions.explanation: Fill raises the shadow side, so the key-to-fill ratio is the dial that sets contrast and therefore the mood of the shot.

questions.prompt: A rim or back light is used mainly to
options: Separate the subject from a similarly toned background
Expose the subject's face correctly
Reduce render noise
Simulate ambient occlusion
questions.explanation: An edge of light along the subject's outline creates a tonal break at the silhouette, which restores depth when subject and background share values.

title: Compositing and Keying
conceptGoal: Understand how alpha, spill and render passes let separate elements combine into one believable image.

questions.prompt: What does an alpha channel store?
options: Per-pixel coverage or opacity used to blend an element over a background
The colour temperature of the shot
The depth of each pixel from the camera
The motion vector of each pixel
questions.explanation: Alpha is the mix factor in the over operation, so it decides how much of the foreground versus background survives at each pixel, including soft edges.

questions.prompt: Why does a green screen key often leave a green fringe on hair?
options: Spill: green light bounced onto the subject and is genuinely in those pixels
The keyer is running at the wrong resolution
The alpha channel is missing
The footage is interlaced
questions.explanation: The fringe is real captured light rather than a keying error, which is why the fix is spill suppression on the colour instead of a harder matte.

questions.prompt: What is a render pass such as ambient occlusion or cryptomatte for?
options: Isolating a component of the render so it can be adjusted in comp without re-rendering
Compressing the output file
Raising the sample count
Converting the scene to a different renderer
questions.explanation: Splitting the image into components moves creative control from the slow render step into the fast comp step, where changes are near-instant.

questions.prompt: Why should compositing operations happen in linear colour space?
options: Light adds linearly, so blends and blurs only behave physically in linear space
Linear space uses less memory
Display space cannot store alpha
It is the only space with 16-bit support
questions.explanation: Display-referred gamma curves are non-linear, so adding or blurring in them produces mathematically wrong values, most visibly on bright edges and defocus.

title: Rigging Basics
conceptGoal: Understand how armatures, weights and constraints turn a static mesh into something posable.

questions.prompt: What does weight painting define?
options: How much each bone influences each vertex when the armature deforms the mesh
The colour of the material at each vertex
The order in which bones are evaluated
Which bones are visible in the viewport
questions.explanation: Deformation is a weighted blend of bone transforms per vertex, so bad weights are exactly why elbows collapse or shoulders tear when the rig is posed.

questions.prompt: When is inverse kinematics preferable to forward kinematics?
options: When the end of a chain must hit a fixed target, such as a foot planted on the ground
When you want each joint rotated independently
When the rig has only one bone
When rendering with motion blur
questions.explanation: IK solves the chain backwards from a goal position, which is precisely what contact points need, while FK is easier for arcs where the end position is unconstrained.

questions.prompt: Why use a control bone separate from the deforming bone?
options: Animators get a clean, selectable interface without touching deformation internals
It halves the file size
Deform bones cannot be keyframed
It is required for rendering
questions.explanation: Separating the animation interface from the deformation rig means the rig's internals can be changed later without breaking animation already made on the controls.

title: Story Structure in Short Form
conceptGoal: Understand how setup, turn and payoff compress into a one-minute piece without feeling truncated.

tutorialRefs.title: Blender Studio — open movies and production insight

questions.prompt: In a one-minute film, what is usually the first thing to cut?
options: Setup the audience can infer from context
The turn
The payoff
All of the ambience
questions.explanation: Audiences fill in exposition automatically from visual context, so setup is the cheapest thing to imply, while removing the turn or payoff removes the story itself.

questions.prompt: What makes an ending feel earned rather than arbitrary?
options: It resolves the specific expectation the setup created
It is the longest shot in the piece
It uses the loudest music
It fades to black
questions.explanation: Satisfaction comes from the answer matching the question that was planted, and without that link any ending is just a stopping point.

questions.prompt: Why is a clear character goal useful even in an abstract piece?
options: It gives the viewer something to track, which creates tension and attention
It shortens the render time
It removes the need for editing
It guarantees a happy ending
questions.explanation: Wanting something creates the possibility of not getting it, and that gap is what holds attention across a sequence of images.

questions.prompt: What does 'show, don't tell' mean practically in an edit?
options: Replace narration explaining a state with an image that demonstrates it
Remove all dialogue from the piece
Use more on-screen text
Always cut to a close-up
questions.explanation: A demonstrated fact is experienced by the viewer and therefore believed, while a stated fact is only received, which is weaker per second of runtime.

title: Delivery and Export
conceptGoal: Understand codecs, containers and colour tagging well enough that the exported file matches what you graded.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a container and a codec?
options: The container such as MP4 wraps streams, while the codec such as H.264 encodes them
They are two names for the same thing
The container compresses and the codec stores metadata
Containers apply only to audio
questions.explanation: A container is packaging that can hold several differently encoded streams, so the file extension alone says nothing definitive about how the video was compressed.

questions.prompt: Why is an intermediate codec preferred over H.264 for a mastering export?
options: It is lightly compressed and intra-frame, so it survives re-encoding and further editing
It produces smaller files
It is the only codec with audio support
It renders faster on every machine
questions.explanation: Delivery codecs throw away data for size and re-encoding those results compounds the loss, so masters are kept in a high-bitrate intra-frame format.

questions.prompt: Your export looks more contrasty than the timeline. The likely cause is
options: A colour space or tagging mismatch between the export and the player
The bitrate was set too high
The audio was exported in stereo
The frame rate is fractional
questions.explanation: If the file is tagged with or interpreted under a different transfer function than it was graded in, the player applies the wrong curve, which shows up as a contrast and saturation shift.
